content.text:
PR #6 is open and mergeable: https://github.com/OrhunMahir/ehl-day-by-day/pull/6. Like the earlier ones it only touches your files, so you can merge it yourself with "Create a merge commit".

**Findings outside both their streams:** there are none. Every finding sits either in Julien's files or in Orhun's, so there was nothing I could fix on their behalf.

Here are the two prompts. Each colleague can paste theirs into their coding agent as is.

---

**For Julien**

> Written for: Julien's coding agent, working in stream J.

```text
Stream I (Ivan) reviewed the package and found issues in stream J's files. Fix them on stream-j (git switch
stream-j, git pull, git merge origin/main first). Edit only stream J's files (browser.py, observe.js, browsing.py,
browsers.py, tests/test_browser*). Details are also in docs/log/ivan.md, latest entry.

1. observe.js, the `clean` function (around line 11): the regex contains raw invisible characters (zero-width
   spaces and the left-to-right/right-to-left marks U+200E/U+200F). Raw direction marks in source are what linters
   and code reviewers flag as obfuscated code, and Atira's AI reviewer reads every package. Write the character
   class with escapes: /[\u200b-\u200f\u2060\ufeff\u00ad]/g. Then check the whole package for raw invisible
   characters (a short Python loop over the files looking for code points 0x200B-0x200F, 0x2060, 0xFEFF, 0xAD,
   0x202A-0x202E, 0x2066-0x2069) and escape any you find in your files.
2. browser.py line 12: OBSERVE_JS is read with read_text() without encoding; on Windows that decodes as cp1252
   and fails. Use read_text(encoding="utf-8").
3. observe.js, `describe` for INPUT: a password input prints its value (value="..."), so a filled login password
   or a TAN typed into a password-type field goes into the model's prompt and the run log. For type=password,
   show only whether it is filled (e.g. value=<filled>/<empty>).
4. browser.py `_HtmlText.handle_endtag`: a stray </script> or </style> makes `skip` negative, and then all later
   text is dropped (the check is `if not self.skip`). Clamp it: self.skip = max(0, self.skip - 1).
5. browser.py `fetch_file`: for an HTML URL the page is fetched once with fetch() and then loaded again in a
   scratch tab, so a GET with side effects (e.g. a logout or cancel link) runs twice. Render the HTML already
   fetched (e.g. set it as the scratch page's content with the URL as base) instead of loading the URL a second
   time, or at least skip the first fetch for HTML.
6. browsing.py `run`: when the model sends several tool calls in one turn and `finish` comes before a `note`, the
   function returns at `finish` and the later note is lost. Run all non-finish calls of the turn first, then
   handle finish.
7. browsing.py `_shows_sign_in`: any visible password field counts as an expired session, so a password-type TAN
   or code field on a normal page triggers an automatic re-login and a jump back to the previous URL. Only treat
   it as a sign-in page if the form also has a user-name field, or the URL looks like a sign-in page
   (_looks_like_sign_in_url), or the page was not a password page before the action.

Add a test for 3, 4 and 6 in tests/test_browser*.py with invented pages only. Run
`uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests` in agent/ (the engine tests must stay green), add a push log entry
to docs/log/julien.md, commit with "J: ..." and push to stream-j.
```

---

**For Orhun**

> Written for: Orhun's coding agent, working in stream O. (I wrote it in English like the code; translate if he prefers.)

```text
Stream I (Ivan) reviewed the package and the engine integration on stream-o and found issues in stream O's files.
First `git merge origin/main` on stream-o: main now has stream I's PR #6 (or merge it when it is merged) with
`result.needed()` and `result.complete`. Edit only stream O's files. Details are also in docs/log/ivan.md, latest
entry.

1. HIGH, agent.py `Orchestrator.price`: the facts are merged by top-level field
   (`{**self.facts_data, **data}`), so a later price_bid that sends only new `materials` (or any other list)
   replaces the whole list and the earlier items are lost; the engine then reports those materials as missing or
   a Kataloggruppe as not searched. Keep a `facts.FactsBuilder` on the Orchestrator instead: `builder.add(data)`
   merges list items by identity (same material number, same mail key + date + sender, ...), merges materials and
   revisions field by field, validates only the update and rejects a bad one whole with the field named (return
   that message to the model). Then `engine.evaluate(builder.facts())`. Use `facts.update_schema()` as the tool's
   parameter schema, so every field is optional and `replace_lists` lets the lead take back wrong records. Log
   `builder.data` instead of `merged`.
2. HIGH, agent.py `without_hasty_no_bid`: every issue other than "no active material matches" counts as an open
   question. Issues like "sender unknown" or "two records with the same date" are common, so in a scenario whose
   correct answer is no_bid the agent would still send a partial bid, and the no_bid decision is worth 75 points.
   The engine itself already refuses a no_bid unless the unmatched requirement's Kataloggruppe was searched. Base
   the check on the checklist instead: keep the no_bid when `result.needed()` has no entry with kind "find" for
   the unmatched positions (or none at all); before submitting a no_bid, have the lead re-check once the values
   the issue names after "closest:".
3. agent.py `price`: return `result.needed()` and `result.complete` with every price_bid result (next to answer,
   issues, incomplete, omitted). In the lead prompt: work through the "find" entries in order (each names the site
   by role, what to read, the rule and the positions; turn them into investigate tasks); "verify" entries are
   checks, not blockers; when `complete` is true, or the time is up, submit.
4. MEDIUM: main still has the old llm.py (fallbacks to the providers' public addresses, a 600 s call timeout);
   stream-o already fixes both. Merge stream-o into main before the next `atira submit`, so a submission never
   carries the old client.
5. LOW, run.py `load_run`: a 200 response whose body is not JSON raises from json.loads instead of being retried;
   treat a JSONDecodeError like a failed attempt.

Run `uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests` in agent/ (the engine tests must stay green), then one local
run with the scouting logins and one sandbox test run; write the points per field (points only, no values) into
docs/log/orhun.md, commit with "O: ..." and push to stream-o.
```

---

One note for Orhun: point 4 matters before the next `atira submit`. Every submission comes from `main`, and `main` still has the old model client until his branch is merged.

        """A "no bid" is final only when every position without a material had its catalogue group searched on
        purpose and the engine asks for nothing more about it. Otherwise those positions are left out and the

content.text:
`main` is in good shape, and all review findings are fixed. But the test runs show the agent still loses almost all position points, and the cause is time, not code errors.

**State of `main`**
- All 9 PRs are merged (2 from you, 5 from Julien, 2 from Orhun), and every stream branch is at the state of `main`.
- All 180 tests pass, including Julien's browser tests and Orhun's former `test_kit` failures, and even without the Windows UTF-8 workaround.
- **Julien fixed all 7 points:**
  - invisible characters written as escapes; a scan of the whole package finds none anymore;
  - UTF-8 when reading `observe.js`;
  - password fields show only "filled" or "empty";
  - the HTML parser survives a stray closing tag;
  - pages are loaded only once;
  - `finish` comes last in a turn, so notes sent with it are kept;
  - better detection of an expired session.
- **Orhun fixed all 5 points:**
  - the lead model now collects facts with `FactsBuilder` (`add_facts`);
  - the no-bid check is based on the checklist;
  - `needed` and `complete` reach the lead model;
  - the model client goes through the proxy only, with a 240-second limit;
  - `run.py` retries a reply that isn't JSON.

**Latest test runs** (points only, no values):

| Run (UTC) | Quality | Positions answered |
|---|---|---|
| 14:17 (2 runs) | 10 / 10 | 0 of 5 |
| 14:35 | 15.2 | 1 of 5, with the right material for the first time |
| 14:48 / 14:51 | 10 / 10 | 0 of 5 |
| 15:10 (2 runs) | still running | – |

The 10 points are the decision and the tender reference. The discount was missed every time.

**Why, from the 14:51 run log** (I only evaluated times and counts):
- **The tender and specification facts are complete:** 5 positions, Q&A, withdrawal, 3 revisions with the current mark, all requirement fields.
- **ERP and mailbox delivered nothing:** 0 materials and 0 mail records in the facts. So the engine had to leave every position out, and the discount stays at 0 % with no approval.
- **The reason is the time plan.** The first ERP sub-agent worked from 55 s to 245 s, then hit its time limit before it was done; it also had to search 5 Kataloggruppen and open 3 transactions per candidate. The mailbox sub-agent had two stalled model calls. At 511 s the lead model sent six more ERP and mailbox tasks, but they all stopped at **512 s, one second later**, because the investigation window was already closed. The rest of the time went to the submission (814–940 s).
- **The lead model recorded facts only once** (`add_facts` 1×), against 11 investigations.

**What the team should look at.** These belong to Orhun and Julien, not your stream:
- **Orhun, time plan:** don't send investigations that start after the window has closed. Give the ERP more time in the first round, or have it work on several Kataloggruppen in parallel tabs; his PR #9 enables that, but at 511 s there was no time left for it. After every report, convert the facts with `add_facts` right away instead of waiting until the end.
- **Julien, ERP sub-agent:** 39 steps in 190 seconds isn't enough for 5 groups with 3 transactions per candidate. The task could be split per Kataloggruppe.

The engine itself isn't the bottleneck right now: it gets too few facts. Should I write these points up as a short message for Orhun and Julien, or wait for the two runs that are going right now? They started at 15:10 with Orhun's latest changes, so they'll show whether the timing problem has already improved.

One caution from my side: while evaluating the log, two log lines containing the site addresses and a partly masked username of an already expired run got printed in this session. The addresses are public, and the run logins are invalid after the run, so practically nothing is exposed. I'll still mask more strictly in future.

SCR="C:/Users/IVANUZ~1/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--Users-Ivan-Uzunov-projects-ehl-day-by-day/63b2d78c-bd7f-45fe-af13-734f4d6272aa/scratchpad"; mkdir -p "$SCR" && cat > "$SCR/runlog.py" <<'EOF'
"""Summarise a run log without printing any value from it: only times, counts and event kinds."""
import collections, json, re, sys

recs = [json.loads(l)["text"] for l in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8") if l.strip()]
lines = []
for t in recs:
    if lines and not re.match(r"^\[\s*[\d.]+s\]|^\[[a-z]", t):
        lines[-1] += t
    else:
        lines.append(t)

def t_of(l):
    m = re.match(r"^\[\s*([\d.]+)s\]", l)
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else None

print(f"log lines {len(lines)}; last timestamp {max((t_of(l) or 0) for l in lines):.0f}s")
print("\n-- lead actions (time, tool, site, size of call / result)")
for l in lines:
    m = re.match(r"^\[\s*([\d.]+)s\] \[lead\] (<- )?(\w+)", l)
    if not m:
        continue
    t, back, tool = m.groups()
    if tool not in ("investigate", "add_facts", "price_bid", "submit_bid", "calculate", "time", "facts", "engine"):
        continue
    site = re.match(r'^\[[^]]*\] \[lead\] investigate \{"site": "([\w-]+)"', l)
    extra = ""
    if back and tool == "investigate":
        extra = " sections=" + ",".join(s for s in ("FOUND", "SUPERSEDED", "CHECKED, NOT PRESENT", "NOT CHECKED") if s in l)
        extra += " from-notes" if "written from notes" in l else ""
        extra += " cut-off" if "cut off" in l else ""
    if back and tool in ("add_facts", "price_bid"):
        extra = " " + ("rejected" if re.search(r"could not|error|Error", l[:400]) else "ok")
        c = re.search(r'"complete": (true|false)', l)
        extra += f" complete={c.group(1)}" if c else ""
        extra += f" finds={l.count(chr(34) + 'find' + chr(34))}"
    print(f"{float(t):6.0f}s {'<- ' if back else '   '}{tool:12} {site.group(1) if site else '':16} len={len(l):6}{extra}")

print("\n-- sub-agents (first..last step, steps, actions, how they ended)")
steps = collections.defaultdict(list)
for l in lines:
    m = re.match(r"^\[\s*([\d.]+)s\] \[([\w.#-]+)\] (\w+)", l)
    if m and m.group(2) != "lead":
        steps[m.group(2)].append((float(m.group(1)), m.group(3)))
for agent, ev in steps.items():
    kinds = collections.Counter(k for _, k in ev)
    ends = [f"{t:.0f}s {k}" for t, k in ev if k in ("finished", "stopped", "cut", "model", "wrap", "session")]
    print(f"{agent:22} {ev[0][0]:5.0f}..{ev[-1][0]:5.0f}s steps={len(ev):3} {dict(kinds.most_common(6))} ends={ends[:6]}")

print("\n-- last facts snapshot (counts only)")
snaps = [l for l in lines if "[lead] facts " in l]
print("snapshots:", len(snaps), "at", [f"{t_of(l):.0f}s" for l in snaps])
if snaps:
    try:
        data = json.loads(snaps[-1].split("[lead] facts ", 1)[1])
        print({k: (len(v) if isinstance(v, list) else bool(v)) for k, v in data.items()})
        mats = data.get("materials", [])
        print("material fields filled:", sorted({k for m in mats for k, v in m.items() if v not in (None, "", [])}))
    except ValueError as e:
        print("snapshot not parseable:", e)
other = collections.Counter()
for l in lines:
    for word in ("stalled", "timed out", "Traceback", "Error", "429", "503", "retrying", "hard stop", "did not finish"):
        if word in l:
            other[word] += 1
print("\n-- trouble words:", dict(other))
EOF

content.text:
The main bottleneck is **model wait time**, not the engine and not the website code. One single call of the lead model hung for **5.4 minutes**, which used up the entire time meant for follow-up investigations. The run was confirmed to use exactly the current `main` code (all 38 files identical).

**Timeline of the run** (15:10 UTC, quality 10, decision and reference right, 4 of 5 positions left out):

| Time | What happened |
|---|---|
| 28 s | The lead sends 4 sub-agents out in parallel (tender, specification, ERP, mailbox). |
| 218–268 s | All four hit their time limit (3 min) before finishing; the ERP agent managed 29 steps. |
| 304–322 s | The reports are converted into facts. |
| **322–647 s** | **The lead model does nothing for 5.4 minutes.** Its next call doesn't come back until 647 s. Meanwhile the fact-recording calls are also too slow ("a recording call took too long"). |
| 647 s | The answer arrives, but the investigation time is already over. The ERP follow-up the lead sends right then gets no time. The agent submits the bid as it stands. |
| 647–870 s | The submission sub-agent fills in the form; the bid is accepted. |

**The result of that:**
- **Facts at the end:** 1 material instead of 5, so 4 positions are left out. From the mailbox, only the discount approval, one metal index and two delivery commitments came through. The end reserves, FX rate, tariffs, setup pool and project bonus are all missing.
- **The ERP is too slow:** about 6.5 seconds per step (model call plus browser action), and 29 steps aren't enough for 5 Kataloggruppen with 3 views per candidate.
- **There was no second round,** because the stalled lead call used up its entire window.

**Probable cause of the stall:**
- Two test runs were started in parallel at 15:10. They share the team's limit of 32 simultaneous Qwen calls, and each run has its sub-agents plus the background fact-recording calls.
- The log shows a rate-limit response (429) and several stalled calls.
- On top of that, the lead's call carries a very large context (brief, facts schema, reports), and Qwen thinks before answering.

**What Orhun should do** (his files):
1. **Limit the lead's calls**, like the sub-agents (75 s, then retry), instead of up to 240 seconds per attempt plus retries. A retry usually comes back quickly.
2. **Don't start test runs in parallel.** The two runs slow each other down through the shared Qwen limit.
3. **Use the time better:** don't let the first round end in a hard timeout. Give the ERP more time, or split it per Kataloggruppe across several tabs, which his PR #9 enables.

**Minor finding:** at the very end the agent crashes with an `AuthenticationError`. Once a bid is accepted, the platform invalidates the run token, and the submission agent makes another model call after that. The bid was already accepted at that point, so it cost nothing. The agent should still stop cleanly once acceptance is confirmed, rather than crash.

The engine part worked correctly in this run: the facts were recorded 7 times, the engine priced them each time, and the one position with a material was calculated.

Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.

The sources agree on the basic mechanism, but none measures how disabling thinking affects tool-calling accuracy in agents.

- **Hard switch:** Setting `enable_thinking=False` provides a hard switch to strictly disable the model's thinking behavior, matching the earlier Qwen2.5-Instruct models. With it off, output contains no think block at all (the model will not generate any think content and will not include a <think>...</think> block.).
- **Latency:** The Qwen docs say this mode is particularly useful in scenarios where disabling thinking is essential for enhancing efficiency. A third-party Ollama tutorial makes the latency point directly, noting that it results in lower latency and higher speed.
- **Serving via API:** In vLLM and SGLang, you pass the flag through chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false} inside the extra_body parameter. Note that this is not OpenAI API compatible. Adding a flag like this matters if your agent client expects a standard OpenAI-style request.
- **Soft switch:** Adding `/no_think` to prompts is a different mechanism. It only applies when thinking is enabled, and the model will follow the most recent instruction in multi-turn conversations. If you need thinking reliably off, the hard switch is the one to use.
- **Tool calling:** Qwen's model card says Qwen3 excels in tool calling capabilities. We recommend using Qwen-Agent. The sources don't say whether tool-call accuracy drops when thinking is off.
- **Sampling:** For non-thinking mode, the recommended settings are Temperature=0.7, TopP=0.8, TopK=20, and MinP=0.

I found no benchmark comparing tool-call success rates with thinking on versus off, so if that matters for your agent, you'd need to test it on your own tasks.

The search covered DOM and accessibility-tree reduction well, but returned nothing on Stagehand's action caching, so that part of your query is unanswered.

**Agent-E and the cost of raw DOM.** A survey of efficient GUI agents describes Agent-E as pushing DOM distillation and denoising, and cites raw DOM inputs reaching about 800k tokens, with typical tasks needing roughly 25 LLM calls ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)). A separate paper notes WorkArena pages running from 40K to 500K tokens, which drives up both inference cost and latency ([arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397)).

**Reduction approaches.**
- **Compressed DOM:** "Beyond Pixels" downsamples DOM snapshots to around 10^3 tokens while keeping hierarchical structure ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)).
- **Retrieval-style pruning:** FocusAgent keeps only task-relevant AxTree lines at each step, cutting the tree by over 50% on average and capping context at 2k tokens ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)). LineRetriever reports 61–73% observation reductions ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)).
- **Accessibility-tree compression:** A11y-Compressor reports cutting input tokens to 22% of the original while raising OSWorld success by 5.1 points on average ([arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397) / [emergentmind.com](https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2605.00551)).

**Latency and evaluation.** One study found that evaluating 11 reduction methods end to end took 232.4 cumulative hours, so it proposes a cheaper proxy metric based on whether the minimal necessary HTML elements survive reduction. That proxy reportedly correlates with end-to-end success and speeds evaluation by over 100x ([catalyzex.com](https://www.catalyzex.com/author/Haochen%20Zhang)). The same work reports a pruning program that makes per-step latency 2.2x faster on WorkArena L1 while retaining 84% of success ([catalyzex.com](https://www.catalyzex.com/author/Haochen%20Zhang)).

**Caching and tooling.** A community MCP middleware claims up to 98% token reduction by filtering to interactive elements, plus in-memory page-state caching and delta diffs between steps. Treat these as vendor claims, not benchmarks ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/Manthan-Railkar/browser-optimizer-mcp-V2)). A separate analysis argues that inference calls, not the browser library, are the main latency bottleneck ([generalcompute.com](https://www.generalcompute.com/blog/browser-agents-inference-speed-as-the-gating-factor?agent=true)).

**Gap:** I found no source on Stagehand's action caching or how it reuses cached actions to avoid LLM calls. A search targeting Stagehand's documentation or changelog would be the next step.

- **Compressed DOM:** "Beyond Pixels" downsamples DOM snapshots to around 10^3 tokens while keeping hierarchical structure ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)).
- **Retrieval-style pruning:** FocusAgent keeps only task-relevant AxTree lines at each step, cutting the tree by over 50% on average and capping context at 2k tokens ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)). LineRetriever reports 61–73% observation reductions ([arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)).
- **Accessibility-tree compression:** A11y-Compressor reports cutting input tokens to 22% of the original while raising OSWorld success by 5.1 points on average ([arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397) / [emergentmind.com](https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2605.00551)).

**Latency and evaluation.** One study found that evaluating 11 reduction methods end to end took 232.4 cumulative hours, so it proposes a cheaper proxy metric based on whether the minimal necessary HTML elements survive reduction. That proxy reportedly correlates with end-to-end success and speeds evaluation by over 100x ([catalyzex.com](https://www.catalyzex.com/author/Haochen%20Zhang)). The same work reports a pruning program that makes per-step latency 2.2x faster on WorkArena L1 while retaining 84% of success ([catalyzex.com](https://www.catalyzex.com/author/Haochen%20Zhang)).

**Caching and tooling.** A community MCP middleware claims up to 98% token reduction by filtering to interactive elements, plus in-memory page-state caching and delta diffs between steps. Treat these as vendor claims, not benchmarks ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/Manthan-Railkar/browser-optimizer-mcp-V2)). A separate analysis argues that inference calls, not the browser library, are the main latency bottleneck ([generalcompute.com](https://www.generalcompute.com/blog/browser-agents-inference-speed-as-the-gating-factor?agent=true)).

**Gap:** I found no source on Stagehand's action caching or how it reuses cached actions to avoid LLM calls. A search targeting Stagehand's documentation or changelog would be the next step.

I ran one search. It found no direct guidance on batching multiple actions per LLM call or running parallel tabs inside one browser-use agent, so those points are not covered here. The results do point to several ways to cut per-step latency, mostly from vendor blogs and one research abstract.

- **Fewer LLM calls:** A plan-then-execute design moves LLM calls to plan generation, which one write-up says cuts browser-agent costs about 50×. It applies mainly to structured, predictable tasks like form fills. Splitting planning from execution into two phases cuts costs 50× by concentrating LLM calls at plan generation only. The efficiency gain applies specifically to structured, predictable web tasks like form fills and OTP extraction.
- **Codifying repeated steps:** TinyFish argues that once a site's steps are learned, code can replace LLM calls. Their figure is that per-step latency falls from 500ms–2s to single-digit milliseconds. This is a vendor claim.
- **Faster models:** Browser Use reports a custom gateway that cut latency about 6x, with the latency shown is pure LLM inference time—just the time the model takes to decide what to do next. Our latency is ~68 seconds per trajectory compared to ~225-330 seconds for other models. These are the company's own benchmarks.
- **Smaller observations:** A research paper reports that pruning HTML gives 2.2× faster per-step latency on WorkArena L1 while retaining 84% of the original success rate. The same paper says extractive HTML reduction needs either high compute cost or domain-specific tuning to reduce latency. The cotomi Act paper combines adaptive lazy observation, verbal-diff-based history compression, coarse-grained actions, and test-time scaling via best-of-N action selection, which is the closest match to your multi-action idea, though it doesn't spell out parallel tabs.
- **Caching limits:** Prefix caching helps less here because the page state changes every step.
- **Parallelism:** TinyFish's parallelism applies across sites rather than within one task. When you need to check 50 sites, sequential execution takes the sum of all task times. With TinyFish's parallel execution, total time equals the slowest single task.

For parallel tabs or batched actions specifically, the browser-use docs or issue tracker would be the next place to check.

import json, sys, statistics
d = json.load(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8")); calls = d.get("calls", d) if isinstance(d, dict) else d
t0 = min(c["at"] for c in calls)
print(" start  latency  queue   input  output  cached  status")
for c in sorted(calls, key=lambda c: -c["latency_ms"])[:10]:
    print(f"{(c['at']-t0)/1000:6.0f}s {c['latency_ms']/1000:7.1f}s {c.get('queue_ms',0)/1000:6.1f}s {c['input_tokens']:7} {c['output_tokens']:7} {c.get('cache_read_tokens',0):7}  {c['status']}")
q = [c.get("queue_ms", 0) for c in calls]
print(f"\nqueue: median {statistics.median(q)/1000:.1f}s, sum {sum(q)/1000:.0f}s | calls with >5s queue: {sum(1 for x in q if x > 5000)}")
fast = [c for c in calls if c["output_tokens"] < 300]; slow = [c for c in calls if c["output_tokens"] >= 1000]
for name, xs in (("output <300 tokens", fast), ("output >=1000 tokens", slow)):
    if xs: print(f"{name:22} n={len(xs):3} median latency {statistics.median(c['latency_ms'] for c in xs)/1000:5.1f}s")
rate = [c["output_tokens"]/((c["latency_ms"]-c.get("queue_ms",0))/1000) for c in calls if c["output_tokens"] > 500 and c["latency_ms"]-c.get("queue_ms",0) > 1000]
print("output speed for long answers: median %.0f tokens/s" % statistics.median(rate) if rate else "")
print("cache read share of input: %.0f%%" % (100*sum(c.get('cache_read_tokens',0) for c in calls)/sum(c['input_tokens'] for c in calls)))
EOF

content.text:
The cause is clear and can be measured. The data covers all 119 model calls of the run (times and token counts only).

## Why the ERP takes so long

**1. The model thinks far too long before ordinary clicks.** In `agent.py` (Orhun's file), both the lead model and every browsing sub-agent run with `reasoning_effort = "xhigh"`, the highest level. Before every click, the model writes out a long chain of thought first. Qwen produces about **41 tokens per second**, so the run looks like this:

| Model calls | Count | Median duration |
|---|---|---|
| short answer (< 300 tokens) | 86 | **3.3 s** |
| long answer (≥ 1,000 tokens, almost all of it thinking) | 17 | **49 s** |
| the lead stall | 1 | **339 s** for 11,930 output tokens |

That's exactly the pattern in the ERP: the first steps take 3.5 s each, then individual steps take 12, 24 or 38 seconds whenever the model "thinks hard". The 5.4-minute lead stall wasn't a network problem either: it was a single answer of nearly 12,000 tokens.

**2. The ERP needs many page views by its structure.** For each Kataloggruppe you need a search, then for each candidate 3 transactions (material, stock, conditions) with sub-tabs (technical data, quantity scales). With 5 groups and about 2 to 3 candidates each, that's 60 to 80 steps. One sub-agent can't manage that sequentially in 3 minutes, even at 3.5 s per step.

**3. Queueing due to two parallel test runs.** 33 calls waited more than 5 s in the platform's queue, 457 s in total. The two runs from 15:10 share the team's limit of 32 simultaneous Qwen calls.

## What we can do, by impact

1. **Switch thinking off for browsing (Orhun, `agent.py`/`llm.py`):** for sub-agents, `enable_thinking: false` via `extra_body.chat_template_kwargs`, the same switch Julien already uses for the wrap-up. Qwen's documentation describes this hard switch for exactly this purpose: more speed. For the lead, a low level plus a `max_tokens` limit (e.g. 2,000), so a 12,000-token answer can't happen at all. That alone should roughly halve step time for most steps and remove the stalls. Whether tool-call accuracy suffers isn't documented anywhere, so a test run should show it.
2. **Parallelise the ERP per Kataloggruppe (Orhun and Julien):** one sub-agent per group in its own tab. Orhun's PR #9 already enables several investigations per site. 5 groups in parallel cost about the time of one. The Kataloggruppen come from the specification report, and my checklist already names them as separate "search Kataloggruppe X" entries, so each can become one ERP task directly.
3. **Fewer page views per candidate (my files):** my filling guide currently says "record every candidate (also inactive ones and near misses)", which drives the agent to open every candidate in full. But the ERP's search list already shows the key attributes in the description line. Better: record attributes from the result list, and open the details (status, stock, conditions, scales) only for the candidates that match the requirement. That saves maybe two thirds of the ERP page views. The engine works the same either way.
4. **Read several pages in one step:** Julien's `read_pages` lets the model fetch several detail pages it picked in one step, e.g. all three transactions of a material at once instead of three separate clicks with three model calls. The prompt should actively encourage that. Research on browser agents ("coarse-grained actions", fewer calls per task) points the same way.
5. **Don't start test runs in parallel,** so the queue doesn't slow us down ourselves.

The research and vendor reports agree that **model latency, not the browser, is the main bottleneck** for browser agents. The usual levers are fewer and shorter model calls, smaller page views, and parallel work. One study reports 2.2× faster steps from pruning page content. Some of these numbers are vendor claims; I'd treat them as direction, not proof.

I can do point 3 right away, since it's my own file (filling guide and checklist text). Points 1, 2 and 4 belong to Orhun and Julien; I'd write prompts for those like last time. Should I go ahead?

Sources:
- [Qwen3 – enable_thinking hard switch (NVIDIA model card)](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/assets/ace/model_card/Qwen3-8B-Instruct.pdf)
- [Qwen3 – enable_thinking via extra_body in vLLM/SGLang (Hugging Face)](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-MLX-8bit)
- [Disabling model thinking for lower latency (Ollama tutorial)](https://deepcharts.substack.com/p/how-to-use-or-disable-model-thinking)
- [Browser agents: inference speed as the gating factor (General Compute)](https://www.generalcompute.com/blog/browser-agents-inference-speed-as-the-gating-factor)
- [Browser Use: LLM gateway and latency](https://browser-use.com/posts/llm-gateway)
- [The hidden latency tax of AI agents (TinyFish)](https://www.tinyfish.ai/blog/hidden-latency-tax-ai-agents)
- [Plan-then-execute cuts browser-agent costs (AI Weekly)](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/plan-then-execute-architecture-slashes-browser-agent-costs-50)
- [Efficient GUI Agents: a systems survey (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02309)
- [Revisiting observation reduction for web agents (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29397)
- [Observation pruning, 2.2× faster steps (CatalyzeX)](https://www.catalyzex.com/author/Haochen%20Zhang)

## exp-speed
"""The model behind the agent, through one OpenAI-compatible client. Switch it with environment variables only:

  AGENT_PROVIDER=qwen       (default) the hosted Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
  AGENT_PROVIDER=anthropic  Claude via Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  AGENT_PROVIDER=openai     OpenAI (e.g. a Codex/GPT model): OPENAI_BASE_URL, OPENAI_API_KEY
  AGENT_PROVIDER=openrouter any OpenRouter model: LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1, OPENROUTER_API_KEY
  AGENT_MODEL=<model id>    overrides the provider's default model

In a run every base URL already points at the platform's metering proxy; your own keys go in team secrets.
"""
import asyncio
import os
import time

from openai import APIError, APITimeoutError, AsyncOpenAI, RateLimitError

DEFAULT_MODELS = {
    "qwen": "qwen3.8-flash-next",
    "anthropic": "claude-sonnet-5-5",
    "openai": "gpt-5.5",
    "openrouter": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
}

# Longest lead call seen in a run was about 90 s; a call that hangs must not eat the run.
CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 240


def _client_config(provider: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Base URL and key of a provider. Every base URL comes from the run's environment, where it points at the
    platform's metering proxy; there is no address to fall back to."""
    env = os.environ
    if provider == "qwen":
        return env["QWEN_BASE_URL"], env["QWEN_API_KEY"]
    if provider == "anthropic":
        return env["ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/v1", env["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
    if provider == "openai":
        return env["OPENAI_BASE_URL"], env["OPENAI_API_KEY"]
    if provider == "openrouter":
        return env["LLM_PROXY_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/openrouter/v1", env["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]
    raise SystemExit(f"Unknown AGENT_PROVIDER {provider!r}; use one of {', '.join(DEFAULT_MODELS)}")


class Model:
    def __init__(self, provider: str | None = None, model: str | None = None, reasoning_effort: str | None = None):
        # how much the model thinks before it answers; None leaves the provider's default
        self.reasoning_effort = reasoning_effort
        self.provider = provider or os.environ.get("AGENT_PROVIDER", "qwen")
        self.model = model or os.environ.get("AGENT_MODEL") or DEFAULT_MODELS[self.provider]
        base_url, api_key = _client_config(self.provider)
        self.client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=base_url, api_key=api_key, timeout=CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, max_retries=0)
        self.calls = 0
        self.prompt_tokens = 0
        self.completion_tokens = 0

    async def chat(self, messages: list[dict], tools: list[dict] | None = None, **kwargs):
        """One completion with retries; returns the assistant message."""

"""What the model client sends: thinking switched off, a token limit, a reasoning level."""
import asyncio
import os
import sys
import unittest
from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import llm  # noqa: E402


class FakeCompletions:
    def __init__(self):
        self.sent = []

    async def create(self, **args):
        self.sent.append(args)
        message = SimpleNamespace(content="ok", tool_calls=None)
        return SimpleNamespace(choices=[SimpleNamespace(message=message)], usage=None)


def sent(model: llm.Model, **kwargs) -> dict:
    fake = FakeCompletions()
    model.client = SimpleNamespace(chat=SimpleNamespace(completions=fake))
    asyncio.run(model.chat([{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], **kwargs))
    return fake.sent[0]


@patch.dict(os.environ, {"QWEN_BASE_URL": "http://127.0.0.1:9/qwen/v1", "QWEN_API_KEY": "local"})
class Thinking(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_thinking_off_for_qwen(self):
        args = sent(llm.Model(provider="qwen", thinking=False, reasoning_effort="xhigh"))
        self.assertEqual(args["extra_body"]["chat_template_kwargs"]["enable_thinking"], False)
        self.assertNotIn("reasoning_effort", args)

    def test_existing_extra_body_is_kept(self):
        args = sent(llm.Model(provider="qwen", thinking=False), extra_body={"top_k": 20})
        self.assertEqual(args["extra_body"]["top_k"], 20)
        self.assertFalse(args["extra_body"]["chat_template_kwargs"]["enable_thinking"])

    def test_token_limit_and_reasoning_level(self):
        args = sent(llm.Model(provider="qwen", reasoning_effort="low", max_tokens=4000))
        self.assertEqual((args["max_tokens"], args["reasoning_effort"]), (4000, "low"))
        self.assertNotIn("extra_body", args)

    def test_a_call_may_set_its_own_token_limit(self):
        args = sent(llm.Model(provider="qwen", max_tokens=4000), max_tokens=500)
        self.assertEqual(args["max_tokens"], 500)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

import asyncio, os, sys, time

"""Same browsing-like question with Qwen's thinking at xhigh and off; prints time and output tokens per call."""
import asyncio, os, sys, time
sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1])
import llm

PAGE = ("[erp] URL: /search\nF4 Materialsuchhilfe\n[3] input(text) name=q value=\"\"\n[4] button \"Suchen\"\n"
        "Hint: search by catalogue group from the specification; at most 20 results.")
TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "type", "description": "Type text into an input; enter submits.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"element": {"type": "string"}, "text": {"type": "string"},
                         "enter": {"type": "boolean"}}, "required": ["element", "text"]}}}]
MSG = [{"role": "system", "content": "You operate a website through numbered elements. Act with tools."},
       {"role": "user", "content": f"Task: search the catalogue group G-TEST-1 in the ERP.\n\n{PAGE}"}]

async def one(label, model):
    t = time.time()
    m = await model.chat(MSG, TOOLS, temperature=0.2)
    calls = [c.function.name for c in (m.tool_calls or [])]
    print(f"{label:22} {time.time() - t:6.1f}s  completion tokens {model.completion_tokens:6}  tool calls {calls}")

async def main():
    await one("warm-up (thinking xhigh)", llm.Model(provider="qwen", reasoning_effort="xhigh"))
    for i in range(2):
        await one(f"thinking xhigh #{i+1}", llm.Model(provider="qwen", reasoning_effort="xhigh"))
        await one(f"thinking off   #{i+1}", llm.Model(provider="qwen", thinking=False))
        await one(f"lead: low, 4000 #{i+1}", llm.Model(provider="qwen", reasoning_effort="low", max_tokens=4000))

asyncio.run(main())
EOF

The changes are on the new branch `exp-speed`, pushed to GitHub. All 184 tests pass. I haven't opened a PR: two of the files belong to Orhun, so he should review them first.

**What's on the branch:**

1. **Less thinking, bounded calls** (in Orhun's files `llm.py` and `agent.py`):
   - Browsing and submission sub-agents think not at all any more, instead of at `xhigh`.
   - The lead model thinks at `low`, with at most 4,000 tokens per answer and 120 seconds per call. If a call stalls, the lead asks again instead of waiting until the end of the run.
   - The facts are recorded by their own model without thinking. Before, that job ran on the lead model at `xhigh`, which caused the 146 s and 166 s calls.
2. **Fewer ERP page views** (your files): the filling guide and the checklist now say to record search results with the attributes the result list already shows, and to open details (status, stock, conditions, scales) only for results that match.
3. **Already on `main`, so nothing to do:** splitting the ERP per Kataloggruppe (Orhun's prompt, 4 tabs per site) and reading several pages in one step (Julien's `read_pages`).

**Measured on the real hosted Qwen** (free local calls through `atira models proxy`, not ranked), the same browsing step:
- thinking `xhigh`: 10.3 s and 12.8 s;
- **thinking off: 2.2 s and 3.0 s**;
- lead setting (`low`, 4,000 tokens): 5.8 s and 5.6 s.

Every variant chose the right tool call. Still open: whether the lead decides as well at `low` as at `xhigh`. Only a test run can show that.

**Your test run of `main`** (`run_118558b27a94dae0`) waited 19 minutes in the queue and has been running since 16:08 UTC. It should finish around 16:28. I'm watching it in the background and will evaluate it as soon as it's done.

After that I'd propose a test run of `exp-speed`, but not in parallel, so the two don't slow each other down. Comparing the two runs then shows directly what the change brings. For Orhun, the push-log entry says which constants and spots in his files to look at.

Links: [{"title":"Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25bx.html"},{"title":"Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/45496"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2409.07429v1"},{"title":"[Literature Review] Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://www.themoonlight.io/review/agent-workflow-memory"},{"title":"[論文評述] Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://www.themoonlight.io/tw/review/agent-workflow-memory"},{"title":"Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://liner.com/review/agent-workflow-memory"},{"title":"Original Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429","url":"https://hub.athina.ai/research-papers/agent-workflow-memory"},{"title":"โ† Back to Paper List","url":"https://papers.lunadong.com/paper/8669"},{"title":"agent workflow memory","url":"https://sotaverified.org/papers/agent-workflow-memory"},{"title":"Agent Workflow Memory","url":"https://mlanthology.org/icml/2025/wang2025icml-agent"}]

The Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) paper, by Wang, Mao, Fried, and Neubig, reports gains on both benchmarks. It was published at ICML 2025.

- **Mind2Web:** AWM raised the baseline success rate by about 24.6% in relative terms. The paper's arXiv version describes this as a 24.6% improvement in relative step-wise success rate on cross-task results.
- **WebArena:** The gain was about 51.1% in relative success rate over the top published autonomous method (Drouin et al., 2024). It also beat a method that used human-written workflows by 7.9%. AWM additionally reduced the number of steps needed to finish WebArena tasks.
- **Method:** AWM induces commonly reused routines from past tasks and supplies them to the agent. It works offline, using training examples, or online, using test queries as they arrive. An supervision-free online variant iteratively induces workflows from self-generated predictions that an evaluator judges correct.
- **Generalization:** Online AWM surpassed baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the gap between train and test task distributions widened.

The sources agree on these figures. The most reliable versions are the ICML proceedings and the arXiv paper (2409.07429). Secondary summaries such as the Moonlight review and the lunadong.com page repeat the same numbers.

AgentOccam is a web agent paper by Ke Yang and colleagues at UIUC and Amazon, published at ICLR 2025. Its core idea is that tuning the agent's observation and action space to match what the underlying LLM was trained on matters more than building elaborate agent strategies.

**WebArena results:** The paper reports that AgentOccam surpasses the previous state-of-the-art and concurrent work by 9.8 (+29.4%) and 5.9 (+15.8%) absolute points respectively. Against similar plain web agents, it boosts the success rate by 26.6 points (+161%), which the authors attribute to its observation and action space alignment.

**Method:** The authors achieve this without using in-context examples, new agent roles, online feedback or search strategies. The benchmark itself covers four common domains: e-commerce platforms (OneStopShop), social forums for idea and opinion exchange (Reddit), collaborative software development (GitLab), and content management, and the paper uses GPT-4-turbo as the base model. The authors also corrected errors they found in some of WebArena's original evaluators, which is documented in their appendix.

**Other benchmark:** On WebVoyager, which uses real-world websites, the paper reports that AgentOccam exceeds the former best agent by 2.4 points (+4.6%) on tasks with deterministic answers.

Sources: the arXiv paper (arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825) and the ICLR 2025 poster page.

Links: [{"title":"mer.vin","url":"https://mer.vin/category/ai/news/page/9/"},{"title":"Anthropic’s Research on GenAI Building Blocks","url":"https://cobusgreyling.substack.com/p/anthropics-research-on-genai-building"},{"title":"when not to build ai agents anthropics workflow vs agent playbook","url":"https://mer.vin/2026/05/when-not-to-build-ai-agents-anthropics-workflow-vs-agent-playbook/"},{"title":"when not to build ai agents anthropics workflow vs agent playbook","url":"https://mer.vin/2026/05/when-not-to-build-ai-agents-anthropics-workflow-vs-agent-playbook/?amp=1"},{"title":"• Biweekly Engineering","url":"https://biweekly-engineering.beehiiv.com/p/building-effective-agents-lessons-from-anthropic-biweekly-engineering-episode-37"},{"title":"Building effective agents","url":"https://scrapbox.io/nikkie-memos/Building effective agents"},{"title":"Anthropic Revealed Secrets to Building Powerful Agents","url":"https://videohighlight.com/v/0v7TQIh_kes"},{"title":"building effective agents","url":"https://www.aihero.dev/building-effective-agents"},{"title":"Engineering at Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents"}]

Anthropic's guide, "Building effective agents," draws a line between workflows and agents, and its main advice is to start simple.

- **The distinction:** Anthropic groups everything under "agentic systems," then separates workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents, where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.
- **Default to simplicity:** The guide recommends finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed, and notes that this might mean not building agentic systems at all.
- **Cost trade-off:** Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, so the choice depends on whether that trade is worth it.
- **Frameworks:** The guide's finding is that the most successful implementations used simple, composable patterns rather than complex frameworks or specialized libraries. A secondary summary says the article warns that frameworks can create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts and responses.
- **Use case fit:** A third-party summary says workflows suit predictability and consistency in well-defined tasks, while agents fit open-ended problems where progress can be verified (such as coding with tests), though that summary is not Anthropic's wording.

The primary source is anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents. The other results are secondary commentary, and one of them is a blog post that appears to be AI-assisted, so I'd rely on the original for specifics.

Links: [{"title":"WAInjectBench: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detections for Web Agents","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.01354"},{"title":"WAInjectBench: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detections for Web Agents","url":"https://alphaxiv.org/abs/2510.01354"},{"title":"BrowseSafe: Understanding and Preventing Prompt Injection Within","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2511.20597v1"},{"title":"WAInjectBench: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detections","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2510.01354.md"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.01354v1"},{"title":"WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks","url":"https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/49781"},{"title":"WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks","url":"https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/121728"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575v3"},{"title":"WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks","url":"https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/REDACTED.html"}]

The search turned up three relevant papers, but nothing that directly measures hidden-text injections against defenses on VWA-Adv and WASP together.

- **WASP (NeurIPS 2025):** This is an end-to-end benchmark for web agent security. Attacks partially succeed in up to 86% of cases, but even state-of-the-art agents often struggle to fully complete the attacker's goals. The paper's abstract doesn't break out a hidden-text or defense-specific number.

- **VWA-Adv:** The attack is described as perturbing product images on e-commerce platforms to trick an agent into posting positive reviews. It is an image-based attack, not a hidden-text one.

- **WAInjectBench (arXiv 2510.01354):** This benchmark tests detectors on text and image injections from VWA-Adv, EIA, and WASP. Its cross-attack results show that domain-adapted detectors often improve detection for the training attack but generalize poorly to others. For example, a detector trained on WASP reached a true positive rate of 0.90 on WASP but scored 0 on the other attacks. The paper also reports that text-based detection outperforms image-based detection for VWA-Adv embedded images when captions include explicit instructions.

- **BrowseSafe (arXiv 2511.20597):** This paper targets injections hidden in web content, such as instructions buried in long comment threads, and proposes a benchmark and prevention approach. I didn't retrieve its specific results.

For VWA-Adv and WASP numbers under specific defenses, the next step would be to read the WASP paper's evaluation tables or the WAInjectBench results directly.

WorkArena is a ServiceNow Research benchmark for LLM-based web agents on enterprise knowledge work, and the main finding is that current agents are far from full automation.

- **Design:** The benchmark runs on a remote-hosted ServiceNow instance and includes 29 tasks in the original paper (ICML 2024 abstract). It ships with BrowserGym, an environment with multimodal observations and a standard action space for designing and evaluating such agents.
- **Later version:** Later sources describe a larger version with 33 tasks across six categories, such as list filtering, form filling, and knowledge-base search (a 2026 blog post summarizing the work). The task count differs between sources, so check which version you need.
- **Key result:** GPT-4o reached a 42.7% success rate. That compares with 6.1% for GPT-3.5 and 17.9% for Llama3, and all models achieved 0% success on list filtering tasks.
- **Conclusion:** The authors say current agents show promise on WorkArena, but a considerable gap remains before full task automation. ServiceNow's own write-up is similarly cautious, saying these agents are not quite ready to substitute humans for enterprise-class use cases.

The paper is arXiv 2403.07718, with the authors listed under McGill University and ServiceNow. These results are from 2024 models, so newer models may score differently.

Links: [{"title":"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v2"},{"title":"www.alphaxiv.org","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/overview/2503.13657"},{"title":"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?","url":"https://nips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/121528"},{"title":"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?","url":"https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/121528"},{"title":"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3"},{"title":"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?","url":"https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/122442"},{"title":"Submitted 26 Oct 2025","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2503.13657v3"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657.pdf"},{"title":"export.arxiv.org","url":"https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657"}]

The MAST paper, "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., Berkeley), is the main result here. Its taxonomy has 14 failure modes in three categories. The category names differ across versions: early arXiv versions say "specification issues," while later versions and the NeurIPS listing say "system design issues." The authors developed MAST through analysis of 150 traces, guided by expert human annotators, with inter-annotator agreement of κ=0.88. They used MAST and the dataset to analyze failure patterns across models (GPT-4, Claude 3, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama) and tasks (coding, math, general agent).

Main findings:
- **Causes are mostly architectural and coordination-related, not just model weakness.** One summary of the paper says failures primarily stem from system design issues and inter-agent misalignment, rather than solely from underlying large language model limitations.
- **Gains over single agents are often small.** The abstract notes that performance gains across popular benchmarks often remain minimal compared to single-agent frameworks.
- **Fixes are not simple.** The authors conclude that identified failures require more sophisticated solutions, highlighting a clear roadmap for future research.

Caveat: the 1,600+ trace count and the "200 tasks" figure appear in different versions of the paper, so check the version you cite. The taxonomy's category and mode-level breakdowns are in the arXiv HTML (v3) and the open-sourced dataset on GitHub and Hugging Face.

Links: [{"title":"par.nsf.gov","url":"https://par.nsf.gov//servlets/purl/10479607"},{"title":"huggingface.co","url":"https://huggingface.co/papers/2211.10435"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10435v2"},{"title":"skip to main content","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10479607-pal-program-aided-language-models"},{"title":"author:\"Madaan, Aman\"","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/search/author:\"Madaan, Aman\""},{"title":"par.nsf.gov","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/search/author:%22Alon,%20Uri%22"},{"title":"PAL: Program-aided Language Models","url":"https://cdnjs.deepai.org/publication/pal-program-aided-language-models"},{"title":"Athina AI Research Agent","url":"https://blog.athina.ai/pal-program-aided-language-models"},{"title":"icml.cc","url":"https://icml.cc/virtual/2023/poster/23864"},{"title":"PAL: Program-Aided Language Models","url":"https://mlanthology.org/icml/2023/gao2023icml-pal/"}]

The PAL paper (Gao et al., ICML 2023) reports that offloading arithmetic to a code interpreter improves accuracy. Its main points:

- **Method:** The LLM turns a word problem into Python steps, and a Python interpreter does the computation. The model only handles decomposition. (The paper's authors describe the LLM reading problems and writing programs as intermediate steps, while a runtime like Python handles the solving.)
- **Motivation:** Chain-of-thought models make arithmetic errors during the solving step even when their decomposition is correct, which is the failure PAL targets (per the abstract, LLMs often make logical and arithmetic mistakes in the solution part.).
- **Breadth:** Results span 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning tasks from BIG-Bench Hard and other benchmarks. The paper reports that code generation plus interpretation leads to more accurate results than much larger models across these tasks.
- **Headline number:** On GSM8K, PAL with Codex reportedly beats PaLM-540B using chain-of-thought by an absolute 15 points top-1 accuracy (state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy).

Sources differ slightly on the exact benchmark count. The arXiv and ICML versions cite 13 tasks, while the earlier preprint version cites 12 (per the DeepAI listing), and that version also reports a 40-point gain over chain-of-thought on a different setting. I'd treat the 13-task, 15-point GSM8K figures from the final paper as the reliable numbers and check the full PDF at arxiv.org/abs/2211.10435 for per-task tables.

The strongest 2025 match for your query is ATLAS, a NeurIPS 2025 paper, with Plan-and-Act as the closest hierarchical planner-executor baseline.

**ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025):** This is a web agent that combines a hierarchical planner with an internal world-model to simulate action outcomes before execution. Its pipeline has a planner that proposes candidate actions, a simulator that predicts their consequences, a critic that picks the best rollout, and a browser executor that carries out the action. The authors report that on the WebArena benchmarks, ATLAS attains state of the art success, exceeding prior reported systems by a large margin. On WebArena-Lite, one result reports ∼63% success compared to 54% for the previously published state-of-the art. Its ablations show that sizable drops occur without the world-model, hierarchical planner, and look-ahead-based replanner.

**Plan-and-Act (ICML 2025):** This framework separates a Planner, which generates structured, high-level plans to achieve user goals, from an Executor that turns those plans into environment-specific actions. The reported WebArena-Lite numbers vary by version. An earlier version cites a state-of-the-art 54% success rate on the WebArena-Lite benchmark, while the later v3 reports a state-of-the-art 57.58% success rate on the WebArena-Lite benchmark as well as a text-only state-of-the-art 81.36% success rate on WebVoyager. The 57.58% figure appears on a third-party aggregator page, so I'd check the arXiv v3 directly.

**Caveats:** These figures come from the papers' own reports and I did not verify them independently. The ATLAS number is also on WebArena-Lite, which is a subset of WebArena, so it isn't a like-for-like comparison with full-WebArena leaderboards. For a current ranking, check the WebArena leaderboard directly, since this search didn't surface one.

The search turned up secondary coverage of Anthropic's September 2025 guide, "Effective context engineering for AI agents," not the original post itself.

**Compaction:** Summarizing a long session and restarting from the summary. One aggregator says Claude Code implements this by passing message history to the model to summarize, preserving architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs. Another source notes that Anthropic recommends tuning compaction prompts on complex traces, starting with recall and then improving precision, because overly aggressive summaries can drop subtle context whose importance only becomes apparent later.

**Structured note-taking:** Keeping persistent notes outside the context window. Coverage describes this as a running log of its progress, like a NOTES.md file or a to-do list, outside the main chat. Anthropic's example is a Pokémon-playing Claude, which maintained precise tallies across thousands of game steps.

**Sub-agent architectures:** A lead agent delegates focused work to sub-agents with clean context windows. One summary says each sub-agent reports back a condensed summary, keeping the main agent focused and efficient.

**Overall principle:** Context is treated as a finite attention budget. Anthropic's bottom line is to do the simplest thing that works.

Caveat: these results are blogs and aggregator summaries. For exact wording, check Anthropic's engineering blog directly.

Links: [{"title":"Structured Extraction","url":"https://neo4j.com/labs/agent-memory/explanation/structured-extraction/"},{"title":"DEV Community","url":"https://dev.to/alexcloudstar/structured-outputs-for-llms-a-developer-guide-2026-gm6"},{"title":"structured outputs","url":"https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/structured-outputs"},{"title":"reliable structured output llms","url":"https://www.ndthuan.com/reliable-structured-output-llms/"},{"title":"Beyond JSON Mode: Getting Reliable Structured Outputs from LLMs in Production","url":"https://tianpan.co/blog/2025-10-29-structured-outputs-llm-production"},{"title":"structured outputs llm production","url":"https://tianpan.co/blog/2025/10/29/structured-outputs-llm-production"},{"title":"Structured Output in Production: Getting LLMs to Return Reliable JSON","url":"https://tianpan.co/blog/2025-11-10-structured-output-production-llms"},{"title":"structured output production llms","url":"https://tianpan.co/blog/2025/11/10/structured-output-production-llms"},{"title":"semantic validation llm outputs","url":"https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/04/15/semantic-validation-llm-outputs"}]

The search returned practitioner blogs and one project doc, with no peer-reviewed benchmarks. The consensus is that constrained decoding fixes syntax and shape, but semantic checks and retries are still needed.

- **Three approaches:** One guide separates prompted JSON, which enforces nothing, from provider-side constrained decoding and tool calling, where the provider validates arguments against a schema. Constrained decoding / JSON mode enforces valid JSON syntax, and in strict variants, the exact schema, at the token-sampling level.
- **Coverage gaps:** One analysis reports that OpenAI's implementation accepts only a subset of JSON Schema, and neither provider's implementation supports the full breadth of real-world JSON Schema.
- **Quality cost:** One author argues that tight constraints can degrade output. When schema constraints eliminate all the high-probability tokens, the model must choose from lower-ranked alternatives.
- **Semantic failures:** A 2026 piece argues that structural validity is necessary, not sufficient. It describes a case where a string-typed amount passed schema checks but was coerced to zero, which is a failure no schema check catches.
- **Layered pattern:** A practitioner guide recommends provider-native structured output as the first line of defense, Pydantic or Zod validators for semantic and cross-field constraints, and a retry loop with error context.
- **Retry mechanics:** An open-source Neo4j agent-memory doc describes retrying with feedback that names the failed field paths, and it treats truncated JSON as a retry trigger. Retries can be costly, though: one source notes that retrying with error messages sometimes works, but burns tokens and latency.

Overall, the sources point to a layered design: constrained decoding for shape, a semantic validation layer for values, and bounded retries with logging. For rigorous reliability numbers, these sources are not enough, so look for primary provider documentation or academic evaluations.

The search turned up the paper that matches your query most closely, but not Agent-E.

**Closest match: evaluator-driven refinement.** The paper "Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement of Digital Agents" uses learned evaluators as the reward signal inside Reflexion. Its reported gain is up to 29% relative improvement for the best GPT-4 WebArena agent. When integrated as the reward function in Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), the evaluator enhances the best-performing GPT-4 WebArena agent's success rate by up to 29% of relative improvement. The evaluators also agree with oracle metrics at a high rate, finding between 74.4 and 92.9% agreement with oracle evaluation metrics. The Reflexion setup itself has three parts: an Actor, an Evaluator, and a Self-Reflection module. The reflection step runs only when the evaluator judges a trial failed, and its output is stored for later attempts.

**Reflection memory on WebArena.** A separate paper on reflection-based memory reports smaller gains. On 70 WebArena tasks, all reflection methods increased the agent's performance over the baseline by +5 points. The larger effect appeared on earlier failures: agents improve by +20 points on previously failed tasks when provided reflections from previously failed trajectories. Previously successful tasks showed some negative transfer, with even the best methods (Summary and Reflection) only reaching 84% SR.

**Caveat on evaluation.** WebArena's own scoring has known problems. A re-evaluation called WebArena Verified audits all 812 tasks, repairs misaligned evaluations and clarifies ambiguous instructions and reports that on the baseline agent it reduces false negatives by approximately 11%. This matters when comparing reflection or verifier results across papers.

**Not found:** No results covered Agent-E specifically, so I can't speak to its self-verification numbers from this search.

The paper is "Thinking vs. Doing: Agents that Reason by Scaling Test-Time Interaction" (NeurIPS 2025, Shen et al.). The search results cover the abstract and headline claims, but not the detailed benchmark numbers.

**Core idea:** The standard approach adds reasoning tokens before each action, which doesn't let an agent gather new information or adjust over time. The authors instead increase the number of interaction steps within a single rollout, which allows exploration, backtracking, and re-planning. Their framing is that interaction scaling is a powerful, complementary axis to scaling per-step compute.

**Prompting alone helps:** Even without any training, prompting-based interaction scaling can improve task success on web benchmarks non-trivially.

**TTI method:** TTI (Test-Time Interaction) is a curriculum-based online reinforcement learning (RL) approach that trains agents by adaptively adjusting their rollout lengths.

**Results:** Using a Gemma 3 12B model, TTI produces state-of-the-art open-source, open-data web agents on WebVoyager and WebArena benchmarks. The authors also report that TTI enables agents to balance exploration and exploitation adaptively.

**Caveat:** I did not find the exact TTI success rates, baseline comparisons, or ablation figures in these results. The NeurIPS poster page, the paper's Hugging Face page (huggingface.co/papers/2506.07976), and the NeurIPS proceedings entry should have them.

The main source is the arXiv paper "The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks" (Cuadron et al., February 2025). It studies how reasoning models behave when they must act in an environment.

- **The core problem:** The authors frame a Reasoning-Action Dilemma, in which models must balance environmental engagement against internal reasoning about potential actions and their hypothetical consequences.
- **The behavior:** They define overthinking as a tendency to favor internal simulation over acting in the environment. Their experiments used SWE-bench Verified, a software-engineering benchmark, and surfaced three recurring patterns: Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, and Premature Disengagement (Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, and Premature Disengagement).
- **The cost:** Across 4,018 trajectories, higher overthinking scores correlate with decreased performance, with reasoning models exhibiting stronger tendencies toward overthinking compared to non-reasoning models.
- **The fix:** A simple intervention, selecting the candidate solution with the lower overthinking score, reportedly improve[d] model performance by almost 30% while reducing computational costs by 43%. The authors note this treats symptoms rather than root causes. They suggest that native function-calling and selective reinforcement learning could help reduce the tendency.

Caveat: the Moonlight review page says its summary was written by AI, so I'd rely on the arXiv abstract and paper rather than the secondary summaries. The results are from SWE-bench software tasks, so generalization to other agentic domains is an open question the authors themselves raise.

The official Anthropic post is in the results, but the snippet only shows its introduction. The performance and token-cost findings come from secondary write-ups.

- **Official post:** Anthropic's engineering post says the team learned lessons about system architecture, tool design, and prompt engineering. The system works by having an agent that plans a research process based on user queries, and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously.
- **Performance:** In internal evaluations, a multi-agent setup with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Sonnet 4 subagents beat a single-agent setup by more than 90 percent (by 90.2% on research tasks). The gain is tied to token usage and to spreading reasoning across separate context windows.
- **Token cost:** One write-up puts the cost at roughly fifteen times the tokens of a standard chat, so the approach fits tasks where the outcome is worth that expense.
- **Parallelism limits:** The approach suits problems that split into parallel lines of research. It is less effective for tightly interdependent work such as coding.

I did not run a second search, so I could not confirm the exact token multiplier or the 90.2% figure against Anthropic's own page.

content.text:
I've found the relevant research. In short: we follow most of the well-supported recommendations. The two biggest gaps are exactly the ones the test runs showed: too much thinking per step, and coordination and timing between the agents.

## What research and practice recommend, and where we stand

| Recommendation | Evidence | Us |
|---|---|---|
| **Leave calculation to code, not the model** | PAL: a model that only decomposes and lets code compute beats much larger models (+15 points on GSM8K) | ✅ Strong: the engine computes every rule deterministically |
| **Compact, model-friendly page view instead of raw HTML** | AgentOccam (ICLR 2025): adapting only the observation and action space gives +29 % over the previous best on WebArena, with no extra agent roles; pruning makes steps 2.2× faster | ✅ `observe.js` produces compact text with numbered elements, tooltips, and no hidden decoys |
| **Planner and executor separated** | Plan-and-Act, ATLAS: hierarchical planning holds the best WebArena-Lite results (54–63 %) | ✅ Lead model plus sub-agents. Unusually for us, the checklist (`needed`) *computes* the plan from the rules |
| **Parallel sub-agents with their own context** | Anthropic's multi-agent research system: +90 % over a single agent, but about 15× the tokens | ✅ One sub-agent per site, several tabs per site |
| **Context engineering: notes, compaction** | Anthropic: notes outside the context, sub-agents with clean context | ✅ `note`, old page views discarded, wrap-up from notes |
| **Layered validation of structured output** | Practice: schema plus semantic checks plus retry naming the field | ✅ `from_dict`/`FactsBuilder` reject with the field name; the engine checks semantically |
| **Defend against hidden instructions structurally** | WASP: attacks partly succeed in up to 86 % of cases; trained detectors generalise poorly (0 % on other attacks) | ✅ Hidden text filtered structurally; authority and date rules in code |
| **Avoid premature giving up** | WebArena: GPT-4 declared 54.9 % of solvable tasks impossible | ✅ No-bid only after a complete search, closest candidates named |
| **Act more instead of thinking longer** | "Thinking vs. Doing" (NeurIPS 2025): more interaction steps beat more thinking per step. "Danger of Overthinking": more overthinking means lower success; choosing the less overthinking answer gave about +30 % with 43 % less compute | ❌ **On `main`, every sub-agent runs at `xhigh`**. That's exactly what the test runs showed (12,000-token answers, 339 s). Fixed on `exp-speed` |
| **Multi-agent failures are mostly design and coordination** | MAST (NeurIPS 2025): most failures come from system design and coordination between agents, not model weakness; often little gain over single agents | ⚠️ Our failure is coordination: the ERP round ends in a timeout, follow-up rounds start after the window has closed, and reports reach the facts late |
| **Simple workflow where the task is predictable** | Anthropic "Building effective agents": start with fixed code paths, add autonomy only where needed | ⚠️ Our task always has the same phases (specification → ERP per group → mailbox per topic → price → sign). The lead model still plans freely |
| **Reusable workflows** | Agent Workflow Memory: +24.6 % (Mind2Web) and +51 % (WebArena) relative, from learned routines | ⚠️ Only partly possible: the final runs on unknown software. Only generic site-type knowledge transfers |
| **Self-check and evaluator** | Evaluator plus Reflexion: up to +29 % relative on WebArena | ⚠️ The facts are checked (checklist), but not systematically whether the filled form matches the answer |
| **Trace analysis instead of guessing** | Practice reports: many errors are easy to fix once traces are analysed (up to +16 % on WebArena) | ⚠️ Only since today (`llm-calls` analysis); not yet a routine |

## What's specific to our case

1. **Time is part of the score.** Benchmarks almost only measure success. For us there's a hard 20-minute limit, and cost × time breaks ties. With Qwen at about 40 tokens per second, thinking costs time linearly, so the advice to act rather than think weighs twice as much for us.
2. **The rules are known in advance, and there's exactly one correct answer.** That's rare in the research, where tasks are open. We can *compute* the plan (which facts are missing) rather than letting the model invent it. That's our biggest structural advantage, and we're only half using it: the checklist exists, but the lead model doesn't systematically turn it into tasks.
3. **The final runs on unknown software.** The Mind2Web results show a clear gap on unseen websites. Learned site routines (like AWM) don't transfer. What transfers is generic knowledge of site types and the site-independent engine.
4. **The sites are deliberately hostile** (decoys, look-alike records, superseded versions, hidden instructions). That's closer to security benchmarks like WASP than to WebArena. Our answer, provenance on every fact plus authority and date rules in code, matches the evidence that structural defences beat detectors.
5. **Fair-play constraints** forbid some of the most effective tricks from practice: fixed click paths, codified site steps ("plan-then-execute" with replay), and crawlers. That's why speed has to come from fewer and shorter model calls and from parallelism, not from scripts.
6. **The ERP is the bottleneck by structure:** 60 to 80 page views for 5 groups, with only 32 parallel Qwen calls for the whole team.

## What I'd do next, in this order

1. **Merge `exp-speed`** (thinking off for sub-agents, lead limited) if a test run confirms it. That has the strongest evidence and directly addresses our measured problem.
2. **Fixed phases instead of a freely planning lead:** specification first, then **one ERP task per Kataloggruppe in parallel**, generated from the checklist. The sub-agent model still navigates itself, so fair play is kept. This addresses the coordination problem MAST names as the main cause of failure.
3. **Local test loop instead of scarce sandbox runs:** local runs with the scouting logins are free and unlimited. Add a short trace analysis of each run (time per role, steps per sub-agent, facts per site), like today's.
4. **Opt in to best of three for the final:** the single best of three attempts counts, which is a cheap form of the evidence that more attempts help (test-time scaling).
5. **Check the form against the answer before signing**, as a final evaluator step.
